The inferential problem
=======================
We can now sample perfectly from an S-I-R epidemic
obeying the stochastic dynamics
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{\emph{Infection: }} & &\text{transition }S\to S-1\,,\; I \to I+1 & \text{ occurs at rate }
    & \alpha \, S\, I\,,
\\
\text{\emph{Removal: }}   & &\text{transition }I\to I-1\,,\; R \to R+1 & \text{ occurs at rate }
    & \beta \, I\,.
\end{aligned}
\]
if we know the population size, the rates \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\),
and all the removal times (the times of "conditioned removals" or `CRemoval`s).
Our CFTP method then generates a perfect sample of times of actual `Infection`s
conditioned on what we know.

But for practical purposes we need to draw inferences about \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\)
given the `CRemoval` times.

A discrete caricature
=====================
Consider a random system of discrete random variables \(X\), \(Z\) and \(\theta\)
corresponding respectively to

* the `Infection` times (represented by \(X\));
* the `CRemoval` times (represented by \(Z\));
* and unknown parameters \(\alpha\) (specific pair-wise infectivity) and \(\beta\) (removal rate),
and perhaps also the initial number of infectives. These parameters are represented collectively by
a list \(\theta\).

(we assume the total population size is known, for the sake of simplicity.)

So we are able to sample from the conditional probability mass function
given \(Z=z_0\) and \(\theta=\theta_0\):
\[
f(x | z_0, \theta_0) \quad=\quad
\frac{p(x, z_0, \theta_0)}{p(z_0, \theta_0)}\,,
\]
based on the definition of conditional probability and using
conventional Bayesian notation of \(f\) for conditional
probabilities and \(p\) for absolute probabilities, and allowing
the (typically lower-case) variable names to indicate the random variables concerned.
We can then write an expression for the conditional probability given
a general \(\theta\) rather than the \(\theta_0\) chosen for our simulation:
\[\begin{aligned}
f(x | z_0, \theta_0)
\quad&=\quad
p(x, z_0, \theta)\times
\frac{1}{p(z_0,\theta_0)}\times
\left(\frac{p(x, z_0, \theta_0)}{p(x, z_0, \theta)}\right)
\\
\quad&=\quad
\frac{f(x, \theta| z_0)\times p(z_0)}{p(z_0,\theta_0)}
\times
\left(\frac{f(x, z_0| \theta_0) \times p(\theta_0)}{f(x, z_0| \theta)\times p(\theta)}\right)
\\
\quad&=\quad
f(x, \theta| z_0)\times
\left(\frac{p(z_0)}{p(z_0,\theta_0)}\right)\times
\left(\frac{f(x, z_0| \theta_0)}{f(x, z_0| \theta)}\right)\times
\left(\frac{p(\theta_0)}{p(\theta)}\right)
\,.
\end{aligned}\]

Consider the three bracketed expressions in reverse order:

1. \(p(\theta_0)/p(\theta)\) is simply a ratio of prior probabilities for
two different values \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta\) for the (two-dimensional vector of)
unknown parameters of interest. This will be specified deriving from expert judgement
of the circumstances in which the data has arisen, and hence is known.

2. \(f(x, z_0| \theta_0)/f(x, z_0| \theta)\) is the likelihood ratio
of \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta\) for a given system of
simulations and observations \(x\) and \(z_0\).
It should be possible to calculate and then to compute this using the pattern of observed
`CRemoval` times and simulated `Infection` times, as a function of
\(\theta_0\) and \(\theta\). We can view it as an inverse weight to apply to
the sample \(x\) from \(f(x | z_0, \theta_0)\).

3. Finally consider \(p(z_0)/p(z_0,\theta_0)\): for a fixed reference parameter \(\theta_0\)
this can be treated as an unknown constant of proportionality.

Perfect simulation with weights
===============================
So the plan is to fix a particular parameter value \(\theta_0\),
and make perfect draws of unobserved infection patterns from \(f(x | z_0, \theta_0)\)
(conditioned on \(z_0\) the observed pattern of `CRemoval`s).

For varying \(\theta\), weight each draw \(x\) (which has probability \(f(x | z_0, \theta_0)\)) by
\[
\left(\frac{f(x, z_0| \theta)}{f(x, z_0| \theta_0)}\right)\times
\left(\frac{p(\theta)}{p(\theta_0)}\right)
\]
where the first factor can be computed for each \(\theta\) as a function of \(x\)
and \(z_0\), while the second factor is a ratio of priors for \(\theta\) and \(\theta_0\).
So each draw \(x\) has _weighted_ probability
\[
f(x | z_0, \theta_0)\times
\left(\frac{f(x, z_0| \theta)}{f(x, z_0| \theta_0)}\right)\times
\left(\frac{p(\theta)}{p(\theta_0)}\right)
\quad=\quad
f(x, \theta|z_0) \times \left(\frac{p(z_0)}{p(z_0,\theta_0)}\right)\,.
\]

Thus, averaging over a number of draws and summing out the marginal values of the
sample \(x\)
we then obtain
a (random) function of \(\theta\) whose expectation is an unknown multiple
\(p(z_0)/p(z_0,\theta_0)\)
of
the posterior distribution for \(\theta\), namely \(f(\theta| z_0)\).
But unknown constants of proportionality can be determined by observing
that the random function integrates to \(1\).
The resolution of this appears numerically feasible, since in the target
problem the argument is two-dimensional.

For values of \(\theta\) which are not close to \(\theta_0\),
the weight may usually be very small
(and just occasionally very large), resulting in very high variances
for the corresponding estimates of \(f(\theta| z_0)\).
However we only need local information
in order to establish a steepest-ascent method (or second-order variant)
to find a _maximum a posterior_ estimate of the unknown parameters \(\theta\).

Having noted this,
in fact in our problem we know
\(\theta\) is two-dimensional, so it may not be overly burdensome
to split the two-dimensional region of interest into smaller patches
within which the variance of weight is controlled. Of course then one
needs some kind of patching argument to get at the unknown normalizer.
There may be interesting things to be said about this patching process,
but we set this aside for now.

Remarks at this stage
=====================
* Check I have got this right! Conditional probability is tricky stuff. 
* Re-write for continuous random variables for the parameters!
* Figure out in detail how to compute the weights -- haven't yet tried this at all.
* Are similar tricks known to Bayesians? I think they may be: I dimly recall
something known (I think) as the exchange formula.
* Work out the patching argument. Even without this, one could develop a procedure
of how to change \(\theta_0\) to maximize the _a posteriori_ probability.
* Implement it. It will need quite a bit of computation: however `Julia`
code is fast!
* Can we do better by doing more sophisticated CFTP? For example, if we can
additionally draw exactly from the posterior distribution of _one_ of the parameters
then this should significantly ease the computational task.


Calculations relevant to optimization approaches^[From email conversation, 05/03/2024]
================================================
Here is an explicit description of what is needed for optimization approaches.

1. Use perfect samples to conduct a plain Monte Carlo estimation of 
the gradient \(f'(\theta | z_0)\) and perhaps the Hessian \(f''(\theta | z_0)\);^[Computationally it may be better to work with gradient and Hessian of \(\log f(\theta | z_0)\).]

2. Use estimates of the gradient \(f'(\theta | z_0)\) to carry out a single step of gradient ascent (or conjugate gradient, using the Hessian as well) towards maximising the function \(\theta \mapsto f(\theta | z_0)\);

3. Repeat using the new \(\theta\) till (by standard criteria for gradient ascent) we have got (approximately) to the maximum of \(f(\theta | z_0)\), which is the MLE equivalently the maximum a-posteriori estimator of \(\theta\) based on a uniform prior.

Sticking to the above notation, let \(x\) denote the (unobserved) infection times, \(z_0\) the observed removal times, and \(\theta = (\alpha, \beta)\) the unknown rate parameters driving the infection. Let \(I_t\) and \(S_t\) denote the numbers of infected and susceptible individuals at time \(t\in[0,T]\). Thus (adding in notation from the draft paper) \(z=(\rho^1,\dots,\rho^n)\) with \(0<\rho^1<\rho^2<\dots<\rho^n\le T\). Let us write \(x = (\tau^1,\dots,\tau^n)\), where \(\tau^i\) is the time of the \(i\)^th^ infection: we are implicitly working under the assumption that exactly one person is infected at time 0, i.e. that \(I_0=1\), and thus \(\tau^1\le 0< \tau^2\).

Varying the expression found in @ONeillRoberts-1999, we can write:^[It would be good to have an intuitive derivation of this or equivalent, perhaps as density with respect to the linear birth-death process model?]

\[\begin{aligned}
f(x, z_0, | \theta)
\quad&=\quad
 \left(\prod_{i=1}^n\beta I_{\rho^i-}\right)\left(\prod_{j=2}^n \alpha S_{\tau^j-}I_{\tau^j-}\right)
\exp \left(-\int_0^T(\alpha S_tI_t + \beta I_t) \mathrm{d}t \right) \,,
\end{aligned}
\]

and so
\[\begin{aligned}
\frac{f(x, z_0, | \theta)}{f(x, z_0, | \theta_0)}
\quad&=\quad
 \left(\frac{\alpha}{\alpha_0}\right)^{n-1} \left(\frac{\beta}{\beta_0}\right)^n 
e^{-(\alpha-\alpha_0)\int_0^T S_tI_t \mathrm{d}t}e^{-(\beta-\beta_0)\int_0^T I_t \mathrm{d}t} \,.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now write
\[
w(\theta | x, z_0) = f(x, z_0 | \theta)p(\theta)
\]
for the unnormalised posterior of \(\theta\) given a realisation \(x\) of the infection times. As explained above, the idea is to fix \(\theta_0\) and make \(N\) perfect draws of the unobserved infection times from \(f(x| z_0, \theta_0)\). Each draw can then be _weighted_ by \[
\left(\frac{f(x, z_0| \theta)}{f(x, z_0| \theta_0)}\right)\times
\left(\frac{p(\theta)}{p(\theta_0)}\right) = \frac{w(\theta | x, z_0)}{w(\theta_0 | x, z_0)}
\]
to produce a Monte Carlo estimate of \(f(\theta|z_0)\), up to an unknown constant of proportionality \(p(z_0)/p(z_0,\theta_0)\):

\[\begin{aligned}
f(\theta|z_0) 
\quad&\approx \quad
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^N f(x_k, \theta | z_0) \\
&= \quad \left(\frac{p(z_0)}{p(z_0,\theta_0)}\right)
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^N f(x_k|z_0, \theta_0)\frac{w(\theta | x_k, z_0)}{w(\theta_0 | x_k, z_0)} \,.
\end{aligned}
\]

Note that \(\theta\) only features in the above via the weight ratio, which takes a simple form, as explained above. Thus to calculate the gradient \(f'(\theta | z_0)\) and the Hessian \(f''(\theta | z_0)\) we just need the corresponding properties of \(w(\theta|x,z_0)\). To ease notation, write \(\langle S,I\rangle = \int_0^TS_tI_t\mathrm{d}t \) and \(\langle I\rangle = \int_0^TI_t\mathrm{d}t \). (Note that these depend implicitly upon the sets of infection and removal times.) 

Assuming that the prior distribution \(p(\theta)\) is sufficiently smooth, 

\[\begin{aligned}
w_\alpha(\theta | x, z_0)
&=\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha}w(\theta | x, z_0) \\
&= f(x,z_0|\theta)\left(p_\alpha(\theta) + p(\theta)\left[\frac{n-1}{\alpha} - \langle S,I\rangle\right]\right) \\
&= w(\theta | x, z_0)\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha}\log p(\theta) + \frac{n-1}{\alpha} - \langle S,I\rangle  \right) \,;\\
w_\beta(\theta | x, z_0)
&= w(\theta | x, z_0)\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\log p(\theta) + \frac{n}{\beta} - \langle I\rangle  \right)\,.
\end{aligned}
\]

Similarly,
\[\begin{aligned}
w_{\alpha\alpha}(\theta | x, z_0)
&= w_\alpha(\theta | x, z_0)\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha}\log p(\theta) + \frac{n-1}{\alpha} - \langle S,I\rangle  \right) \\
&\qquad + w(\theta | x, z_0)\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha^2}\log p(\theta) - \frac{n-1}{\alpha^2}\right) \,; \\
w_{\beta\beta}(\theta | x, z_0)
&= w_\beta(\theta | x, z_0)\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\log p(\theta) + \frac{n}{\beta} - \langle I\rangle  \right) \\
&\qquad + w(\theta | x, z_0)\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta^2}\log p(\theta) - \frac{n}{\beta^2}\right) \,; \\
w_{\alpha\beta}(\theta | x, z_0)
&=  w_\beta(\theta | x, z_0)\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha}\log p(\theta) + \frac{n-1}{\alpha} - \langle S,I\rangle  \right) \\
&\qquad + w(\theta | x, z_0)\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha\partial\beta}\log p(\theta)\right) \\
&= \frac{w_\alpha(\theta | x, z_0)w_\beta(\theta | x, z_0)}{w(\theta | x, z_0)}+ w(\theta | x, z_0) \frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha\partial\beta}\log p(\theta)\,.
\end{aligned}
\]

{{< pagebreak >}}

Note that (for example)
\[\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha}\log w(\theta | x, z_0) 
\quad&=\quad
\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha}\log p(\theta) + \frac{n-1}{\alpha} - \langle S,I\rangle  \,,
\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\log w(\theta | x, z_0) 
\quad&=\quad
\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\log p(\theta) + \frac{n}{\beta} - \langle I\rangle  \,.
\end{aligned}
\]
which may be easier to deal with!
